fields.meta_title: Field Service Automation for Dispatch and Visits | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build field service automation that dispatches calls, closes work orders on a phone, moves arrival windows, and books plan visits.
fields.h1: Build Field Service Automation for Your Office and Crews
fields.hero_description: Build field service automation that sends each call to the right technician and closes work orders from a phone.
fields.features_heading: What Field Service Automation Runs for You
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the workflows together with the job records behind them. Diagnosis and repairs stay with your technicians.
fields.feature_1:
Calls matched by zone and certification

Each request from your booking form carries a zip code and a job type. The app offers it to the closest technician certified for that work, then the next one, until someone accepts.
fields.feature_2:
Work orders closed at the customer's door

A technician logs parts and labor against the job on a phone, then hands it over for the customer's signature. The closed work order stays with its job and its customer record.
fields.feature_3:
Customer emails that follow the schedule

The app emails a customer when the technician heads out, and again if the arrival window moves. Each email names the technician and the window, and every send is logged on the job.
fields.feature_4:
Maintenance visits that book themselves

Store each plan's visit dates, and the app opens the work order ahead of each one and assigns the home's usual technician. You pick how many days ahead the work order appears.
fields.feature_5:
Parts and labor synced to QuickBooks

The app connects to QuickBooks, Xero or any tool with an API and sends each closed job's parts and labor lines across for billing. Every job's history sits in a database you own.
fields.feature_6:
The whole app's code in your GitHub

Export the full code of your field service app to your GitHub repository on paid plans. A developer can add a parts catalog or a customer portal and keep the work in your own repo.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Jobs the Office Stops Doing by Hand
fields.tab_content_1:
No-heat calls go to the nearest furnace tech first

Dunnachie Heating and Air books repair calls through a form on its website. At 7:12 AM a no-heat call comes in from the north zone. The app offers it to Zbigniew Pazmino, the furnace-certified technician with an open slot there, and he has 15 minutes to accept before the dispatcher hears about it in Slack.
fields.tab_content_2:
A signed work order closes from the technician's phone

Ikechukwu Sarkissian replaces a furnace igniter on work order WO-4471. On his phone he adds 2 photos and logs an $86.00 igniter, a $24.00 flame sensor and 1.5 labor hours at $95.00. The homeowner signs on the same screen. The app closes the job and sends the $252.50 total to QuickBooks.
fields.tab_content_3:
Any job 30 minutes over moves its next customer's window

Florimond Gruszka's 1:00 PM repair runs 45 minutes past its booked time. Once a job is 30 minutes over, the app shifts the next visit by the full overrun. Rhoswen Cuthbertson, his 3:00 PM customer, gets an email with a new arrival window of 3:45 PM to 5:45 PM, and the dispatch board marks her visit late.
fields.tab_content_4:
Each plan visit due in 21 days gets its work order

Dunnachie sells a maintenance plan with a spring and a fall tune-up. Every Monday the app checks all 118 plans. A visit due within 21 days becomes a work order for the technician who serviced that home last. This week 9 visits qualify, and office manager Eulalia Brennagh sees them on one list to confirm times.

fields.howto_title: How to Build Field Service Automation
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to set up field service automation for one office job, test it on last week's calls, and then add the next.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List what the office does by hand
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Pick the job with the clearest trigger
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Export your customer and job lists
fields.howto_step_1_des: List the tasks your office repeats each morning: offering calls to technicians, chasing paperwork after a job, phoning customers when a crew runs late, and booking plan tune-ups. Note who owns each task today and how many phone calls it takes.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Start with a task that begins on one event, such as a new booking or a closed work order. Write its rule with real numbers: how many minutes a technician gets to accept, or how far over a job can run before the next customer hears.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Put customers, technicians, and open jobs into one spreadsheet. Give each technician a zone and their certifications, and give each customer an address and any plan dates. Dispatch can match a call to a technician only when those columns are filled in.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Tell Emergent what starts the workflow, the rule it follows and who gets told. Emergent builds the workflow and the screens your technicians and dispatcher use. A follow-up prompt changes any number in the rule, such as 20 minutes to accept instead of 15.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Connect QuickBooks and Slack through their APIs, and set up the sender for customer emails. Book a test call through the website form and accept it as a technician. Then close a test work order and check that its lines arrive in QuickBooks.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Run last week's calls and jobs through the app before it contacts anyone. Compare each offer and each window change with what the office did at the time. Look hard at any mismatch: a missing certification or a zone drawn too wide shows up here.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Build the second workflow on the tables the first one fills. Closed work orders already record which technician worked at each home, and the maintenance plan workflow uses that record to assign every tune-up to the right person.
fields.hero_prompt: Build field service automation for my HVAC company that dispatches calls, closes work orders on a phone, and books plan visits.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up field service automation?

plan.angle: The top 10 are field service software vendors (Oracle, ServicePower, Skedulo, Salesforce, allGeo) and list posts that define the term and list features without showing a single rule an operator could switch on. This page follows one HVAC contractor through four jobs the office does by hand, each with its trigger, its numbers and who hears about it: a no-heat call offered to the nearest furnace-certified technician with 15 minutes to accept, a work order closed on the phone with parts, labor and a signature that syncs to QuickBooks, a job 30 minutes over its booked time that moves the next customer's arrival window, and plan visits due within 21 days turned into work orders.
tab_stories: A no-heat call booked on Dunnachie Heating and Air's website at 7:12 AM is offered to Zbigniew Pazmino, the furnace-certified technician with an open slot in the north zone, and he has 15 minutes to accept before the dispatcher hears about it in Slack.

Ikechukwu Sarkissian closes work order WO-4471 on his phone with two photos, an $86.00 igniter, a $24.00 flame sensor, 1.5 labor hours at $95.00 and the homeowner's signature, and the app syncs the $252.50 total to QuickBooks.

Florimond Gruszka's 1:00 PM repair runs 40 minutes past its booked time, and because any job 30 minutes over moves the next visit, the app emails Rhoswen Cuthbertson a new arrival window of 3:30 PM to 5:30 PM.

Every Monday the app checks 118 maintenance plans, and each plan visit due within 21 days becomes a work order for the technician who serviced that home last; this week 9 qualify and office manager Eulalia Brennagh sees them on one list.
